exercise.title: Why does an antiderivative evaluate a definite integral?

statement.p: Part II says that if F'=f, then \int_a^b f(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a). In your own words, why should the total change in an antiderivative equal the accumulated amount of f from a to b?

hint.p: The accumulation function A(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt is one antiderivative of f. Any other antiderivative differs from A by a constant, so endpoint subtraction forgets that constant.

subsection.title: Why the interval hypothesis matters
subsection.p: Part II requires one antiderivative on an interval containing the whole interval of integration. We cannot use an antiderivative formula across a break where the function is not defined.

note.title: Moral
note.p: Endpoint subtraction is allowed only when the antiderivative is valid on one interval covering the whole trip from a to b.

exercise.title: Why must the antiderivative cover the whole interval?

statement.p: Blindly subtracting -1/x from -1 to 1 for \int_{-1}^{1}(1/x^2)\,dx produces a negative number for a positive integrand. In your own words, why does Part II refuse to jump across a break where the integrand is not defined?

hint.p: Endpoint subtraction is legal only when one antiderivative is valid on a single interval covering the whole trip from a to b. Continuity of the integrand on that interval is the safe first check.

subsection.p: The word net matters. Positive and negative changes can cancel.

exercise.title: Why is the integral of a rate a net change?

statement.p: The net change theorem says \int_a^b F'(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a). In your own words, why does that recover final amount minus initial amount, and why does the word net matter when the rate changes sign?

hint.p: Positive and negative rates cancel in the integral. The result is the leftover change, not the total of all upward and downward motion counted as positive.

statement.p: Suppose the temperature of a metal plate changes at the rate
Find the net temperature change from t=0 to t=5.
The rate T'(t) becomes negative after t=3. So the temperature first rises, then falls. The integral counts both effects with signs.

exercise.title: Why are displacement and distance different integrals?

statement.p: If v(t) is velocity, then \int_a^b v(t)\,dt is displacement, while \int_a^b |v(t)|\,dt is total distance. In your own words, why does the first integral allow cancellation, and why must the second refuse it?

hint.p: Displacement is net change of position. Distance counts every piece of motion as positive, so backward motion cannot cancel forward motion.

note.title: Reading Part II in words
note.p: If F accumulates f, then f is the rate of change of F. The integral of f from a to b gives the change in F from a to b.

statement.p: Part II gives a practical method for definite integrals, but it depends on a new skill: finding antiderivatives.
That skill becomes its own language.
